<reason>A ran a sharp, disciplined line: the motion's purpose is disease prevention, donor-egg IVF already achieves it, so MRT's marginal spend buys relatedness plus reversion risk. B's strongest counter was the PGD precedent—health systems already fund genetically related disease-free children—and A conceded PGD funding is legitimate, retreating to "it is rationed," which B correctly reframed as an argument about how to fund rather than whether. A's most damaging remaining point (for homoplasmic mothers, MRT failure yields a sick child rather than no pregnancy) was met by B's staged, registry-tracked funding and the natural-conception counterfactual; A's reply to that counterfactual was clipped, and A's "that's a trial, I never opposed trials" concession sits uncomfortably close to conceding that public systems should fund MRT in a tracked form. B thus kept a clearer live route on the motion as written; A's rhetoric was crisper but its principle eroded under pressure. Both sides suffered clipping and both stayed epistemically disciplined.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's Q2 and [B4.1]–[B4.2]: forcing A to accept PGD funding's legitimacy, then arguing MRT is "PGD's continuation for the patients PGD cannot serve," which converted A's "fertility service" category from a disqualifier into a funding template. A's counter that PGD differs in kind (failure = no pregnancy vs. a sick child) was the sharpest reply, but B's staged-funding answer left it as a design question rather than a reason to vote CON.</best_rebuttal>
